title: Ch. 6 Lecture Slides
description: Original exam-style questions from Dr. Letendre's Chapter 6 slides and the Week 6 lecture.

tech.title: Was Canada in a technical recession?
tech.body: In May 2026 Statistics Canada's initial release showed real GDP growth of **−0.25%** in 2025Q4 and **−0.04%** in 2026Q1. Over 2022–24, GDP growth rates were revised by 0.14 percentage points on average.

clo.title: A closed economy
clo.body: Consider a closed economy (billions of dollars): **Y = 900, C = 520, G = 180, T = 190, TR = 60**.

questions.prompt: According to the Chapter 6 slides, which statement about real GDP per capita is correct?

options.text: It is the most common, albeit imperfect, measure of living standards, so real GDP must grow faster than the population for living standards to rise
It is a perfect measure of living standards because it is adjusted for inflation
It rises whenever real GDP rises, whatever happens to population
It measures the business cycle only and says nothing about long-run growth

questions.explanation: The slides call real GDP per capita the most common, **albeit imperfect**, measure of living standards. Since it is real GDP divided by population, real GDP has to grow **faster than population** for it to rise.

questions.prompt: Real GDP was $2,340 billion in 2024 and $2,415 billion in 2025. What was the growth rate of real GDP in 2025? (percent, one decimal)
Growth in real GDP was 2.4% in one year, −3.0% in the next and 3.6% in the third. Using the slides' method, what was the approximate annual growth rate over the three years? (percent)
questions.explanation: Over a few years the slides average the annual growth rates: (2.4 − 3.0 + 3.6) ÷ 3 = 3.0 ÷ 3 = **1.0%**.

questions.prompt: According to Dr. Letendre's Chapter 6 slides, where are the determinants of long-run growth (textbook pp. 155–156) and potential GDP / the output gap covered?

options.text: Determinants of long-run growth in Chapter 8; potential GDP and the output gap in Chapter 7
Determinants of long-run growth in Chapter 7; potential GDP and the output gap in Chapter 8
Both are covered in Chapter 6, as in the textbook
Neither is covered in this course

questions.explanation: Slide 6 lists the deviations from the textbook: the **determinants of long-run growth move to Chapter 7** (economic growth in greater detail) and **potential GDP / output gap move to Chapter 8**.

questions.prompt: Business cycle theory is concerned with explaining which of the following?

options.text: The permanent upward trend in real GDP per capita
Why population grows over time
Short-run fluctuations of real GDP around its trend
How the central bank sets the level of potential GDP

questions.explanation: The slides separate the upward **trend** (long-run growth, studied in Ch 7) from the **short-run fluctuations around trend**, which business cycle theory tries to explain (causes include oil price shocks, monetary policy, financial crises, pandemics).

questions.prompt: Which statement about the dating of recessions is correct?

options.text: Statistics Canada officially declares when Canadian recessions begin and end
The Bank of Canada officially dates recessions in Canada, and the NBER does so in the U.S.
In Canada no official body dates recessions; the C.D. Howe Business Cycle Council does it unofficially, while in the U.S. the NBER is the official authority
In both countries a recession begins automatically after two quarters of positive inflation

questions.explanation: Statistics Canada produces the data but **does not declare recessions**. The C.D. Howe Business Cycle Council dates Canadian cycles, but it is not an official authority; the **NBER** is the official authority in the United States.

questions.prompt: On the initial May data and the two-quarter rule, what would you conclude?

options.text: Canada was not in a technical recession because only one quarter was negative
Canada was definitely in a deep recession because GDP fell for two quarters
The data cannot be used because Statistics Canada does not produce real GDP numbers
Canada was in a technical recession in 2025Q4 and 2026Q1, but the small decline in 2026Q1 could easily be revised away

questions.explanation: Two consecutive negative quarters meet the technical definition, so the initial data implied a technical recession. But a −0.04% print is smaller than a typical revision (0.14 pp), so many economists **did not rush to declare a recession**.

questions.prompt: If the −0.04% growth for 2026Q1 is revised up by the average revision of 0.14 percentage points, what is the revised growth rate? (percent)
questions.explanation: −0.04% + 0.14% = **+0.10%**. The quarter turns slightly positive, so Canada did **not** have two consecutive negative quarters (the lecture notes this is exactly what happened).

questions.prompt: The C.D. Howe Business Cycle Council declares a recession when a downturn is persistent, pronounced and pervasive. Which of these correctly matches the three dimensions?

options.text: Persistent = duration; pronounced = amplitude (depth); pervasive = scope (how widespread across the economy)
Persistent = scope; pronounced = duration; pervasive = amplitude
Persistent = amplitude; pronounced = scope; pervasive = duration
Persistent = inflation; pronounced = unemployment; pervasive = interest rates

questions.explanation: The three P's map to **duration** (persistent), **amplitude** (pronounced) and **scope** (pervasive). The Council (like the NBER) looks at many indicators: real GDP, employment and output across sectors.

questions.prompt: What typically happens to the inflation rate over the business cycle?

options.text: It rises during recessions because firms raise prices to cover losses
It tends to rise during expansions (especially toward the end) and fall during recessions
It is constant over the business cycle
It falls during expansions as supply catches up with demand

questions.explanation: In expansions demand is high relative to supply, so prices rise faster; in recessions demand is low relative to supply, so inflation falls and prices may even fall (deflation).

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly contrasts stocks and bonds?

options.text: A stock is partial ownership with no maturity date and may pay dividends; a bond is a loan with a fixed maturity date promising to repay a fixed amount
A stock is a loan that must be repaid on a fixed date; a bond represents partial ownership of a firm
Stocks and bonds both have maturity dates, but only bonds pay dividends
Both are forms of ownership; the difference is only the issuing firm's size

questions.explanation: **Stock** = partial ownership, a permanent claim that does not mature; holders may receive dividends and the price reflects expected profitability. **Bond** = essentially a loan from a household to a firm with a fixed maturity.

questions.prompt: You buy a 4-year coupon bond for $2,500 with a 4% annual coupon rate. In the final (fourth) year, how many dollars do you receive in total (final interest payment plus principal)?
questions.explanation: Coupon = 4% × $2,500 = $100 each year. In year 4 you receive the $100 interest **plus the $2,500 principal** = **$2,600**.

questions.prompt: A discount bond is best described as a bond that…

options.text: pays interest each year and repays the face value at maturity
represents partial ownership and pays dividends
is issued by banks and can be withdrawn at any time
pays no periodic interest and is issued below its face value, with the full face value repaid at maturity

questions.explanation: Unlike a coupon bond, a **discount bond** pays no interest during its life; the investor's return is the difference between the low purchase price and the face value received at maturity.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is a financial intermediary rather than a financial market?

options.text: A mutual fund that pools household savings and invests them in stocks and bonds
The stock market
The bond market
A firm's retained earnings

questions.explanation: Financial markets (stock and bond markets) connect savers to firms directly. **Financial intermediaries** (banks, mutual funds/ETFs, pension funds, insurance companies) channel funds from households to firms indirectly. Retained earnings are the firm's own profits, not part of the financial system.

questions.prompt: What is investment I in this economy ($ billion)? (Y = C + I + G)
questions.explanation: I = Y − C − G = 900 − 520 − 180 = **$200 billion**. Since S = Y − C − G, national saving is also $200 billion.

questions.prompt: What is public saving in this economy ($ billion)? (Negative if a deficit.)
questions.explanation: S<sub>public</sub> = T − G − TR = 190 − 180 − 60 = **−$50 billion**, a budget deficit. (Check: S<sub>private</sub> = Y + TR − C − T = 900 + 60 − 520 − 190 = 250; 250 − 50 = 200 = I.)

questions.prompt: In a closed economy, the government raises transfer payments TR by $10 billion, with Y, C, G and T unchanged. What happens to saving?

options.text: Private saving is unchanged and public saving falls by $10 billion, so total saving falls by $10 billion
Private saving falls by $10 billion and public saving is unchanged
Private saving rises by $10 billion, public saving falls by $10 billion, and total saving is unchanged
Public saving rises by $10 billion because the government spends more

questions.explanation: S<sub>private</sub> = Y + TR − C − T rises by 10; S<sub>public</sub> = T − G − TR falls by 10. **TR cancels out of total saving** (S = Y − C − G), so S and I are unchanged.

questions.prompt: In the slides' market for loanable funds, which statement is correct?

options.text: Demand for loanable funds rises as the interest rate rises; the central bank sets the equilibrium rate
Supply of loanable funds comes only from foreign lenders
The relevant interest rate is the nominal rate, which makes the model independent of inflation
Firms' demand falls as the interest rate rises; private saving rises as the interest rate rises; and the equilibrium real rate is determined by borrowers and lenders, not set by an authority

questions.explanation: Demand comes from firms financing investment (fewer projects are profitable at higher rates); supply comes from household and government saving (private saving rises with the rate). The **real** interest rate adjusts so that quantities demanded and supplied are equal; **no authority sets it** (wk 6 slide 12).

questions.prompt: Technological change makes investment projects more profitable. In the loanable funds market…

options.text: supply shifts right, so the real interest rate falls and the quantity rises
demand shifts right, so the real interest rate and the quantity of funds loaned both rise
demand shifts left, so the real interest rate and quantity fall
demand shifts right, so the real interest rate falls and the quantity rises

questions.explanation: More profitable projects raise firms' **demand** for loanable funds (Figure 6.4). With supply unchanged, equilibrium moves up the supply curve: **higher real rate, more funds**.

questions.prompt: Workers become worried about losing their jobs and increase their saving. In the loanable funds market…

options.text: supply shifts left, so the real interest rate rises and the quantity falls
demand shifts right, so the real interest rate and quantity rise
supply shifts right, so the real interest rate rises and the quantity rises
supply shifts right, so the real interest rate falls and the quantity of funds rises

questions.explanation: Higher saving at every interest rate is an **increase in supply** (Figure 6.5): the equilibrium real rate falls and the quantity of loanable funds (saving = investment) rises.

questions.prompt: How do the slides (and Hubbard) treat a government budget deficit in the market for loanable funds, and what is crowding out?

options.text: The government borrows from households, which reduces national saving and shifts supply left; the real rate rises and private investment falls (crowding out)
The government adds to demand for loanable funds; the real rate rises but private investment is unaffected
The deficit shifts supply right because the government is spending more; the real rate falls
A deficit has no effect on the market for loanable funds when the economy is closed

questions.explanation: Slide 26: a deficit means **lower public (and national) saving**, so supply of funds available to firms shifts **left**. The real interest rate rises and private investment falls: higher government spending 'crowds out' private expenditure including investment. A surplus does the opposite.

questions.prompt: Tech firms are borrowing massive amounts to build infrastructure for generative AI. Using the loanable funds model (nothing else changes), the effect on the real interest rate and the quantity of loanable funds is…

options.text: The real interest rate falls and the quantity of loanable funds increases
The real interest rate rises and the quantity of loanable funds decreases
The real interest rate rises and the quantity of loanable funds (saving and investment) increases
The real interest rate is unchanged because only demand changes

questions.explanation: Heavy borrowing for AI infrastructure is an **increase in the demand for loanable funds** (right shift). Along an unchanged supply curve, the equilibrium real interest rate and quantity both rise; since S = I, saving and investment rise too.

questions.prompt: The proposed Productivity Mega Deduction lets businesses immediately write off 100% of the cost of eligible capital property. Considering only its effect on firms' investment incentives (no change in the deficit), what happens in the loanable funds market?

options.text: Demand shifts right (higher after-tax profitability of investment), raising the real interest rate and the quantity of loanable funds
Supply shifts right, lowering the real interest rate and raising the quantity
Demand shifts left (higher after-tax profits make firms borrow less), lowering the real interest rate
Neither curve shifts because taxes do not affect investment decisions

questions.explanation: A tax break that lets firms deduct capital costs at once raises the **after-tax return** on investment projects, so firms demand more loanable funds at every rate: **D shifts right** and both i and L rise. (If the lost tax revenue widened the deficit, supply would also shift left, pushing the real rate up even more.)

questions.prompt: Forecasters now predict that a recession is coming, and borrowers and lenders believe them. What happens in the loanable funds market (assuming only the expected profitability of investment changes)?

options.text: Demand shifts right, so the real interest rate and the quantity of loanable funds both rise
Demand shifts left, so the real interest rate and the quantity of loanable funds both fall
Supply shifts left, so the real rate rises and the quantity falls
Demand shifts left, so the real interest rate falls and the quantity rises

questions.explanation: This is the mirror image of textbook problem 2.10 (expansion forecast → D right). A recession forecast lowers the **expected profitability** of new plant and equipment: **D shifts left**; equilibrium moves down along S: lower real rate and less saving and investment.

questions.prompt: Savers are taxed on nominal interest income. If the government switched to taxing only the real interest income, what would happen in the loanable funds market?

options.text: Demand shifts right: firms borrow more because inflation is lower
Supply shifts left: savers pay less tax and so save less
Supply of loanable funds shifts right: the after-tax real return to saving rises, so the real interest rate falls and saving and investment rise
Nothing, since only the nominal rate matters for the real market

questions.explanation: Taxing real rather than nominal interest raises savers' **after-tax real return** at any real rate, so households save more: **S shifts right**; equilibrium real rate falls and the quantity of loanable funds (saving and investment) rises.
